questions.q: In a tree data structure, what are nodes called that have no children?
options: Root nodes of the tree.
Internal branch nodes with subtrees.
Leaves of the tree.
questions.fact: The topmost node is the root, and nodes with no children are called leaves.
why: The root is the topmost node, not a childless node.
Internal nodes have at least one child node attached.
Nodes having zero children are termed leaf nodes or leaves.

questions.q: How is the height of a tree defined?
options: The number of edges on the longest path from root to leaf.
The total number of vertices present in the entire tree structure.
The maximum number of children attached to any single internal node.
questions.fact: The height of a tree is the number of edges on the longest path from the root to a leaf.
why: Height counts the edge hops from the root to the deepest leaf.
The total number of vertices is the size of the tree.
The maximum number of children per node is the tree's branching factor.

questions.q: What relationship must hold for all keys in a binary search tree?
options: Left descendants are larger and right descendants are smaller than node.
Left descendants are smaller and right descendants are larger than the node.
All nodes at the same level must store identical numeric keys.
questions.fact: The binary search tree property states that all left descendants are smaller and all right descendants are larger than the node.
why: This reverses the BST ordering property; left must be smaller.
For every node, all left keys are smaller and right keys larger.
Keys on the same level are not required to be identical.

questions.q: What is the worst-case search time complexity when a binary search tree is completely skewed?
options: O(1) time because pointers jump directly.
O(log n) time because height stays balanced.
O(n) time because the tree behaves like one long chain.
questions.fact: If a binary search tree becomes completely skewed, its height becomes n and search takes O(n) time.
why: Trees do not have direct index arithmetic to achieve O(1) lookup.
O(log n) requires balanced height; skewed trees have height n.
A completely skewed tree behaves like a linked list of length n.

questions.q: What is the time complexity of inserting a node into a balanced binary search tree?
options: O(log n) by following the search path to an empty spot.
O(1) by placing the node directly as a new root.
O(n) because all existing elements must be shifted in memory.
questions.fact: Inserting a node in a binary search tree follows the search path to an empty spot and takes O(log n) time when balanced.
why: Traversing the logarithmic height of a balanced tree takes O(log n) steps.
Insertion must maintain BST order, not simply replace the root.
Tree nodes are linked via pointers, so existing nodes do not shift.

questions.q: In what sequence does an inorder tree traversal visit nodes?
options: Current node, left subtree, then right subtree.
Left subtree, right subtree, then current node.
Left subtree, current node, then right subtree.
questions.fact: Inorder traversal visits left subtree, current node, then right subtree.
why: Visiting the current node first is preorder traversal, not inorder.
Visiting the current node last is postorder traversal, not inorder.
Inorder traverses left subtree first, visits node, then right subtree.

questions.q: How do preorder and postorder tree traversals differ in visit order?
options: Preorder visits children first, while postorder visits the current node.
Preorder visits the current node before its children, while postorder visits children first.
Preorder processes nodes level by level, while postorder traverses down branches.
questions.fact: Preorder traversal visits the current node before its children, while postorder visits children first.
why: Preorder visits the current node first, not the children.
Preorder processes node before subtrees; postorder processes subtrees before node.
Level-by-level traversal is breadth-first search, not preorder or postorder.
